data.topology_port_debug: Port mapping debug data in topology snapshot
data.topology_panel_all_users: Show topology panel to all users
data.wifi_rf_lists_at_start: Channel and TX power limits at start (wifi_rf_lists_at_start)
data.wifi_rf_every_n_polls: Extra RF reads every N polls (wifi_rf_every_n_polls)
data.traffic_sysfs_fallback: Interface counters from sysfs as fallback (traffic_sysfs_fallback)
data.time_machine_enabled: Network Time Machine for all routers (time_machine_enabled)
data.time_machine_clients: Client histories in the Time Machine (time_machine_clients)

data_description.extended_wifi_sensors: Enables all per-radio, per-SSID (AP) and per-port sensors of this router at once instead of one by one. Turning it off disables only the sensors this switch enabled; sensors you disabled yourself are never touched. Takes effect after about 30 seconds.
data_description.topology_port_debug: Include the raw per-port mapping trace (FDB/DHCP/ARP matches and assignment reasons) in the topology snapshot endpoint. HA diagnostics always stay redacted.
data_description.topology_panel_all_users: Makes the Network Topology sidebar panel and its snapshot API available to every Home Assistant user, not only administrators. The topology contains DHCP leases, ARP/switch tables, the WAN IP and DDNS details. The panel is shared by all routers: it is open to all users as soon as one router has this enabled.
data_description.config_backup_enabled: Allows the configuration backup of this router (all config.* capabilities and the optional ACL tier 'config_backup_read'). Off by default. The switch is shown once a configuration provider (backup engine) is installed or while it is on; without a provider it has no effect. Turning it off stops every backup, probe and comparison for this router at once; stored versions stay. Warning: a backup contains ALL router secrets: /etc/shadow (password hashes of every router login, including root), private keys (SSH host keys, VPN and TLS keys) and the Wi-Fi, VPN and DDNS passwords.
data_description.config_backup_schedule: Daily: one backup per day at the time below; each router starts at its own fixed offset of up to one hour, so they never run at the same time. Off: only manual backups and drift versions. Has an effect only while the configuration backup is on.
data_description.config_backup_time: Local time of Home Assistant. A daily run missed while Home Assistant was off is made up later the same day.
data_description.config_drift_check: Compares the router with its last version when the polled data shows a configuration-near change (5 minutes after the change, at most once per hour). A detected change is saved as a new version (at most four per day). Off: no drift checks.
data_description.wifi_rf_enabled: Evaluates the Wi-Fi radios of this router (utilization, noise, conflicts, client quality, recommendations). Off by default. On its own it uses only the data the integration already polls and adds no router call; each extra read below has its own switch. Nothing is ever changed on the router and no scan is started.
data_description.wifi_rf_get_status: Reads hostapd get_status once per radio every N polls to compute the real channel utilization from busy-time counters. About 0.5 KB per radio and read. Needs wifi_rf_enabled.
data_description.wifi_rf_assoclist: Reads iwinfo assoclist once per access-point interface every N polls for retries, failed frames and connection time of clients. About 0.9 KB per connected client. Needs wifi_rf_enabled.
data_description.wifi_rf_lists_at_start: Reads the allowed channels and TX power steps of each radio once at start and again only after a channel or country change, never in the regular poll. About 2-4 KB per radio. Needs wifi_rf_enabled.
data_description.wifi_rf_survey: Later stage: reads iwinfo survey every N polls only after a capability check passed. The current router ACL does not grant this read; without the right it stays 'not ready' and nothing else is affected. On ath10k radios a survey can block the driver for up to 3 seconds. Needs wifi_rf_enabled.
data_description.wifi_rf_every_n_polls: Cadence of the extra reads above (1-60, default 5). With the 60-second poll, 5 means every 5 minutes; a smaller N never reads more often than every 5 minutes per radio. The reads pause while the router is throttled or on the SSH fallback. Small routers like the FRITZ!WLAN Repeater 1750E (54 MB RAM) should keep 5 or more.
data_description.traffic_enabled: Measures the traffic of this router (WAN, ports, interfaces, VLANs, Wi-Fi clients) from the counters the integration already polls, shows it in the Traffic Analytics tab and adds the traffic sensors. Off by default. Clients appear only as pseudonyms, never with MAC address or host name. Switching off removes the traffic entities of this router; the stored history is kept. Each extra read below has its own switch.
data_description.traffic_station_detail: Reads iwinfo assoclist per access-point interface at most every 5 minutes to fill in client counters the regular poll lacks. Needs traffic_enabled and the module key of the enterprise core.
data_description.traffic_sysfs_fallback: Reads interface counters from /sys/class/net at most every 5 minutes, only for interfaces the regular poll does not list. Needs traffic_enabled.
data_description.traffic_offload_probe: Reads the firewall flow offloading setting (uci get) every 6 hours, because offloaded traffic bypasses some counters. Needs traffic_enabled.
data_description.traffic_history_profile: Compact (default): 5-minute values for 6 hours, hourly for 14 days, daily for 31 days, no client history on disk. Standard: 5-minute values for 1 day, hourly for 14 days, daily for 90 days, client history kept (daily for 30 days); needs more storage. The deepest profile among the routers with traffic on applies to the whole fleet.
data_description.time_machine_enabled: One switch for the whole fleet: switching it here switches it for every router. Shows past events on one timeline in the panel: those the existing modules keep (audit log, configuration versions, network intelligence, Security Center) and its own history of outages, gaps, radio, uplink and configuration changes, kept for 14 days in a store of its own (at most 15000 marks, 2.5 MB). Off by default. No extra router call. MAC addresses, IP addresses, host names and SSIDs are never stored; MAC addresses, IP addresses and SSIDs are never shown. A host name is shown only to administrators, only with client histories on, and only while Client Stability still knows the client. Users who are not administrators see infrastructure and disruptions only, and only while the panel is open to all users. Switching it off stops recording and deletes all stored client histories at once, even if the client history switch stays on. The history of outages, gaps and changes stays stored; while the Time Machine is off it is not trimmed, only after the next switch-on again to 14 days.
data_description.time_machine_clients: Separate switch, one for the whole fleet, off by default; only works while the Time Machine is on and Client Stability runs. Records which client was connected when, to which router and band, roaming and disconnects, for 14 days. Clients are stored only as pseudonyms (tmc_…), never with MAC, IP address, host name or SSID; at most 200 marks per client and day. Only administrators see client histories; the current host name is shown to them while Client Stability still knows the client. Switching this off deletes all stored client histories.
data_description.self_healing_enabled: One switch for the whole fleet: switching it here switches it for every router. On by default. Records and analyses the root incidents of Network Intelligence and recommends only (Observe mode); readable by the panel's API, the panel tab follows in a later release. It never changes a router: no router call of its own, no Home Assistant service and no entity. Records keep router ids, incident ids and cause codes only, never MAC addresses, IP addresses, host names or client names, in a store of their own (at most 500 records, 1 MB). Only administrators see the records; other users see counts only, and only while the panel is open to all users. Switching it off stops the module; the stored records stay.

user.title: Connect to OpenWrt Router
user.description: Enter the connection details for your OpenWrt router. The router must have rpcd and uhttpd running.

data_description.host: Hostname or IP address of the router (e.g. 192.168.1.1)
data_description.protocol: Connection protocol (HTTPS Self-Signed recommended for most OpenWrt routers)

checklist.title: Check Router Configuration — {host}

data.deploy_acl: Set up permissions automatically (deploy ACL via ubus + restart rpcd)

data_description.deploy_acl: Writes the rpcd ACL file to the router via ubus and restarts rpcd. If the router blocks ubus file access, an SSH fallback with the same credentials is attempted. Permissions are re-checked afterwards.

reauth_rpcd_setup.title: rpcd Not Responding on {host}
reauth_rpcd_setup.description:
The router **{host}** is blocking authentication — rpcd may not be configured.

SSH into the router and run:

`opkg update && opkg install rpcd rpcd-mod-rpcsys && uci set rpcd.@rpcd[0].socket='/var/run/ubus/ubus.sock' && uci set rpcd.@rpcd[0].timeout=30 && uci commit rpcd && service rpcd restart`

Then click **Submit** to retry.

reauth_cannot_connect.title: Router Unreachable: {host}
reauth_cannot_connect.description:
Cannot reach **{host}**. Make sure the router is powered on and reachable on the network.

Click **Submit** to retry.

reauth_confirm.title: Re-authenticate with OpenWrt Router
reauth_confirm.description: The credentials for **{host}** (user: {username}) are no longer valid. Please enter the new password.

error.cannot_connect: Unable to connect to the router. Check the host, port and protocol, and ensure the router is reachable.
error.invalid_auth: Authentication failed. Check the username and password.
error.invalid_host: Invalid host address. Use a valid IP or hostname.
error.timeout: Connection timed out. The router may be unreachable or overloaded.
error.unknown: An unexpected error occurred. Check the Home Assistant logs for details.
error.rpcd_setup_required: rpcd is not configured on this router. SSH into the router and run: opkg update && opkg install rpcd rpcd-mod-rpcsys && uci set rpcd.@rpcd[0].socket='/var/run/ubus/ubus.sock' && uci set rpcd.@rpcd[0].timeout=30 && uci commit rpcd && service rpcd restart
error.acl_deploy_failed: Automatic ACL deployment failed — the router rejected ubus file/write and the SSH fallback did not succeed. Deploy the ACL manually using the SSH commands shown above, then run the check again.
error.acl_deploy_no_change: The ACL file was written, but the permissions did not change after re-checking. rpcd may not have finished restarting or required packages are missing — see the install commands above, then try again.
error.acl_already_current: The ACL file on the router is already up to date — the missing permissions have another cause (missing packages or a pending rpcd restart). See the install commands above.
error.acl_tiered_kept: The router has a newer, tiered access list (ACL). It was kept; the old automatic ACL was not written over it. Rights for new features are granted through the core's ACL offer.
error.acl_check_transient: The router could not be reached to check its access list (ACL). Nothing was changed; try again when the router is reachable.

state.not_permitted: Not readable (rpcd ACL or no logd)

time_machine_invalid_mac.message: That is not a valid MAC address.

acl_base_rights_missing.title: Kept rpcd ACL of {router} lacks read rights
acl_base_rights_missing.description:
The rpcd ACL on router {router} is a tiered ACL that an admin approved, so Home Assistant keeps it and does not overwrite it. It lacks {count} read right(s) the integration needs:

{rights}

Sensors that use them may stay unavailable or fall back to SSH. To fix it, deploy a current tiered ACL through an approved ACL offer, or remove `{path}` on the router: the integration then deploys its standard ACL at the next start (the optional tiers are gone until they are approved again).

This message disappears once the deployed ACL grants these rights again.

channel_plan_conflict.title: Wi-Fi channel conflicts between OpenWrt routers
channel_plan_conflict.description:
{count} channel conflict(s) were found across your OpenWrt routers:

{findings}

- `same_channel`: two radios use the same primary channel and have to share airtime.
- `overlap`: the channel widths overlap, for example 40 MHz on 44 and 48, or 160 MHz on 36, which covers 36–64.
- `non_standard_24`: a 2.4 GHz radio is not on channel 1, 6 or 11 and overlaps with its neighbours.

Give neighbouring access points different, non-overlapping channels or narrower channel widths in their wireless settings. DFS channels are not a conflict; they are listed in the diagnostic sensor "Channel plan findings" of each router.

This message disappears automatically once the conflicts are gone.

installation_key_lost.title: OpenWrt Router: installation key lost
installation_key_lost.description:
The installation key of the OpenWrt Router integration is missing or unreadable, while {versions} stored configuration version(s) exist. The key protects the secret digests in these versions; without it, secrets in old and new versions cannot be compared, so drift checks do not report changed passwords or keys.

The integration never creates a new key on its own. An administrator has to request a key reset and a second step has to approve it (critical action). After the reset, the next drift check of every router stores the current configuration as the new baseline.

If you restored Home Assistant from a backup, check first whether the file `.storage/openwrt_router.installation_key` was part of it. Restoring that file and restarting Home Assistant clears this message.

installation_key_replaced.title: OpenWrt Router: installation key replaced
installation_key_replaced.description:
The installation key file of the OpenWrt Router integration was unreadable or unusable. No stored configuration version used it, so a new key ({key_id}) has been created.

If you did not expect this, check the Home Assistant storage folder (`.storage/openwrt_router.installation_key`) and the disk for damage. The core's security log contains the event `core.installation_key_replaced`.

This message disappears after the next restart of Home Assistant.

lan_unreachable.title: No OpenWrt router reachable
lan_unreachable.description:
All {count} OpenWrt routers ({routers}) have been unreachable from Home Assistant since {since}.

When every router fails at the same moment, the cause is almost always between Home Assistant and the LAN (network of the HA host, switch, cabling, VLAN), not in the routers themselves.

This message disappears automatically as soon as a router answers again.

ram_high.title: High memory usage on OpenWrt router {router}
ram_high.description:
The router {router} has been running low on memory since {since}: {pressure} % of its RAM cannot be made available any more, only {available_mb} MB is left (attribute `pressure_pct` of the memory usage sensor).

This message appears when more than 85 % of the RAM is unavailable or less than 16 MB is available for 15 minutes. If it stays like this, the router starts killing processes or reboots. A typical cause is a process that keeps growing (for example rpcd on older firmware). Check `top` or `ps w` on the router and restart the affected service or the router.

This message disappears automatically once less than 80 % of the RAM is unavailable and at least 16 MB is available again.

router_unreachable.title: OpenWrt router {router} unreachable
router_unreachable.description:
The router {router} has not answered since {since} (error type: {error_type}).

Check power, cabling and the rpcd/uhttpd services on the router.

This message disappears automatically as soon as the router answers again.

create_config_backup.name: Create configuration backup
create_config_backup.description: Saves a new configuration version of the selected OpenWrt routers, one after another. Needs the configuration backup switched on for each router. Only a changed configuration creates a new version for scheduled runs; a manual backup is always kept.

device_id.name: Router
device_id.description: One or more OpenWrt router devices of this integration.

note.name: Note
note.description: Optional note stored with the version (at most 200 characters, no control characters). Never put passwords here.

time_machine_forget_client.name: Time Machine: forget a client
time_machine_forget_client.description: Deletes every Time Machine mark of one client (administrators only). Give the MAC address or the pseudonym, exactly one of both. A client that is connected right now is recorded again from its next connect or move. Other modules keep their own client data; the answer lists them. The client counts of the past (state at a moment, comparison) drop by this client, and nothing marks those moments as changed.

mac.name: MAC address
mac.description: MAC address of the client. The Time Machine only uses it to find the pseudonym and does not store it, but Home Assistant itself may keep the action call with the MAC in its log or recorder. Use the pseudonym to avoid that.

client.name: Pseudonym
client.description: Pseudonym of the client as the Time Machine shows it (tmc_ followed by 16 hex digits). No MAC address leaves your input.

time_machine_clear_history.name: Time Machine: clear history
time_machine_clear_history.description: Deletes the Time Machine's own history (administrators only). The other modules keep theirs.

clients_only.name: Client histories only
clients_only.description: Delete only the client histories and keep outages, radio and configuration marks.
